# kyrrð

> Real photographs of Reykjavík taken on foot, the true story behind each one,
> and a free digital postcard you can sign and send. Everything here is free to
> read and free to send. Nothing is stock, nothing is generated: every picture
> was taken on a phone by the person who walked there, in whatever weather the
> day gave.

Facts are checked on location. When something turns out to be wrong it is
corrected rather than quietly left, and monuments missing from the maps have
been added to them.

## Field notes
- [Ólafur Thors Statue, Reykjavík: six times prime minister](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/olafur-thors): Ólafur Thors stands by Tjarnargata beside the Reykjavík pond. He led Iceland six separate times, more than anyone in the country’s history, and the bronze is the work of Sigurjón Ólafsson. Free to visit, in the open, at any hour.
- [The Settlement Pillars, Reykjavík: the stone that steams](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/settlement-pillars): A rough basalt pillar in downtown Reykjavík marks where, by the old story, Ingólfur’s high seat pillars washed ashore and the city began. A steel pipe beside it breathes real steam from the ground. It was missing from Google Maps until 2026, when we added the pin.
- [Looking Seawards (Horft til hafs), Reykjavík harbour](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/looking-seawards): Looking Seawards, in Icelandic Horft til hafs, is a pair of bronze fishermen in oilskins on the shore by the old harbour. Ingi P. Gíslason made it in 1997, marking eighty years since Reykjavík finished its harbour and the sixtieth Day of the Seaman. Open shore, free at any hour.
- [Shore Piece (Fjöruverk): the polished boulders on Sæbraut](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/shore-piece): Shore Piece, in Icelandic Fjöruverk, is a run of fifty five or fifty six boulders polished to a mirror shine among the rough rocks of the Sæbraut seawall. Sigurður Guðmundsson made it in 2002, and the only marker is a small green plate on one of the stones. Free, on open shore.
- [Leif Eiríksson Statue at Hallgrímskirkja, Reykjavík](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/leif-eriksson): The statue of Leif Eiríksson was a gift from the United States and stood on the hill for thirteen years before anyone began building Hallgrímskirkja behind it. Everyone assumes the statue was placed in front of the church; it was the other way round.
- [Jón Sigurðsson Statue, Austurvöllur, Reykjavík](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/jon-sigurdsson): Jón Sigurðsson stands on a column in the middle of Austurvöllur with his face turned to the parliament. He argued Iceland out of Danish rule in print rather than in arms, and the republic chose his birthday, the seventeenth of June, for its national day. Einar Jónsson made the statue, unveiled in 1911.
- [Ingibjörg H. Bjarnason Statue, Reykjavík](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/ingibjorg-bjarnason): Ingibjörg H. Bjarnason was the first woman elected to Iceland’s parliament, in 1922, and the statue beside the Alþingi was the first full statue of a named woman ever raised in Reykjavík. Ragnhildur Stefánsdóttir made it, unveiled on the nineteenth of June 2015, a hundred years to the day after Icelandic women won the vote.
- [Víkurgarður: the oldest burial ground in Reykjavík](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/vikurgardur): Víkurgarður is the burial ground of the first Reykjavík church and the oldest marked ground in the city, in use until 1838. Three grey standing stones carved with faint human figures and no names were given to the city in 2000 to mark it. It is a small open park off Aðalstræti.
- [The Höfði Lighthouse, Reykjavík: built in 2019](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/hofdi-lighthouse): The bright yellow lighthouse on the platform by Höfði looks a century old and was built in 2019. The architects at Yrki Arkitektar followed the pattern of the channel lights raised in Reykjavík’s old harbour between 1913 and 1917. It has no ships to guide; its job is memory. Free, on open shore.
- [Jón Vídalín Bust at Dómkirkjan, Reykjavík](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/jon-vidalin): Jón Vídalín took the bishop’s seat at Skálholt in 1698, and his book of house sermons, printed in 1718 and known as Vídalínspostilla, was the most read book in Iceland after the Bible for two hundred years. The bust beside Dómkirkjan was raised in 1920, two centuries after his death.
- [Séra Bjarni Jónsson Bust at Dómkirkjan, Reykjavík](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/sera-bjarni): Séra Bjarni Jónsson served Dómkirkjan for forty one years, from 1910 to 1951, and Reykjavík made him an honorary citizen. Sigurjón Ólafsson modelled the bust in the cathedral itself, in the real vestments rather than a studio, and it was set beside the church seven years after Bjarni died.
- [A Piece of the Berlin Wall in Reykjavík, by Höfði](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/berlin-wall): A painted slab of the Berlin Wall stands on the lawn by Höfði. It was sent to Reykjavík because the two men who started the Wall’s fall met in the white house a few steps away in 1986. It is three and a half metres tall and free to visit.
- [The Cellist (Tónlistarmaðurinn) at Harpa, Reykjavík](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/cellist): The bronze cellist in the water by Harpa is Tónlistarmaðurinn, the Musician, made in 1970 by Ólöf Pálsdóttir. She modelled it on the cellist Erling Blöndal Bengtsson, who played for hours while she worked, and left the cello without strings on purpose. It moved to the harbour in 2014.
- [Öndvegissúlur at Höfði: the high seat pillars](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/ondvegissulur): Öndvegissúlur stands on the Höfði grounds: a dark column crowned with carved copper, Sigurjón Ólafsson’s monument to the high seat pillars Ingólfur Arnarson threw into the sea and followed ashore. It was raised in 1971. Sigurjón never named it; an art historian did, and the name stuck.
- [Himinglæva, the wind harp outside Harpa, Reykjavík](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/wind-harp): Himinglæva is a stainless steel wave outside Harpa, strung like a harp and played by the wind. Elín Hansdóttir drew its form from a Lissajous figure, the pattern light traces off vibrating tuning forks, and named it for the wave in Norse myth that lets the sky shine through. It arrived on the square in 2022.
- [Christian IX Statue, Government House, Reykjavík](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/christian-ix): Christian IX of Denmark stands on the Government House lawn with one arm held out, handing over the constitution he brought to Iceland in 1874, the country’s first written frame of government. Einar Jónsson made the statue, unveiled in 1915. The lawn is open at any hour.
- [Hannes Hafstein Statue, Government House, Reykjavík](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/hannes-hafstein): Hannes Hafstein became the first Icelander to govern Iceland when home rule arrived in 1904, and the statue stands on the lawn of the building he worked in. He was known as a poet first, and he pushed through the telegraph cable that tied the island to the world in 1906. Einar Jónsson made it, unveiled in 1931.
- [Government House, Reykjavík: a prison turned seat of power](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/government-house): The white house at the foot of Arnarhóll was raised between 1765 and 1770 as the country’s prison, and it now holds the office of the prime minister and the cabinet. It is one of the oldest buildings in Reykjavík. You cannot go inside, but it stands on the street with no fence or gate.
- [Skúli Magnússon Statue, Fógetagarðurinn, Reykjavík](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/skuli-magnusson): Skúli Magnússon became the first Icelander appointed fógeti, the king’s steward, in 1749, and founded the Innréttingar workshops around Aðalstræti in the early 1750s. Historians mark those workshops as the point where the town of Reykjavík actually began. His statue stands in Fógetagarðurinn.
- [Úr álögum, Einar Jónsson sculpture garden, Reykjavík](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/ur-alogum): Úr álögum, out of the spell, stands in the sculpture garden behind the Einar Jónsson museum on the hill by Hallgrímskirkja: a hero lowering his sword over a beaten shape, with the freed figure at his side. Einar gave his whole body of work to Iceland on condition a house be built to hold it. The garden is free all year.
- [Ingólfsgarður Lighthouse, Reykjavík old harbour](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/ingolfsgardur-lighthouse): The small yellow lighthouse at the end of Ingólfsgarður marks the mouth of Reykjavík’s old harbour, the gap every boat passes through. The harbour was built between 1913 and 1917; before that the boats were hauled up onto the beach. You can walk out to the light along the breakwater.
- [Íslandsvarðan on the Sæbraut shore path, Reykjavík](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/islandsvardan): Íslandsvarðan, the cairn of Iceland, sits on the Sæbraut shore path a short way from the Sun Voyager. It looks like a lump of lava and is cast bronze, the work of Jóhann Eyfells, and the opening at its centre frames Mount Esja across the bay. Free, on open shore, and easy to walk past.
- [Dómkirkjan: the cathedral of Reykjavík on Austurvöllur](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/domkirkjan): Dómkirkjan on Austurvöllur is the cathedral of Reykjavík, not Hallgrímskirkja up on the hill. It was built between 1787 and 1796 and holds a marble font carved by Bertel Thorvaldsen. Every new session of the Alþingi opens with a service here, and the members walk from its door to the parliament.
- [Einar Benediktsson Statue at Höfði, Reykjavík](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/einar-benediktsson): Einar Benediktsson stands with a harp beside Höfði, the house he lived in for a dozen years. He was a poet, a lawyer and the founder of Iceland’s first daily newspaper, and the story that outlived his schemes is that he once tried to sell the northern lights. Ásmundur Sveinsson finished the statue in 1964; the city moved it here in 2015.
- [Ingólfur Arnarson Statue on Arnarhóll, Reykjavík](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/ingolfur-arnarson): The bronze settler on Arnarhóll is Ingólfur Arnarson, the man the sagas place at the start of the Icelandic story, landing around the year 874 and naming the place Reykjavík, the bay of smokes. Einar Jónsson made the statue and it went up on the hill in 1924, with the harbour laid out below.
- [The Black Cone, Austurvöllur: the 2009 protest memorial](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/black-cone): The Black Cone is a boulder split by a heavy black cone, standing in the corner of Austurvöllur in front of the Icelandic parliament. Santiago Sierra made it, unveiled in 2012 on the third anniversary of the Pots and Pans protests of 2009, and the plaque carries a line from the French Revolution on the right to refuse.
- [Monument to the Unknown Bureaucrat, Reykjavík](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/unknown-bureaucrat): Iceland has no tomb of an unknown soldier, so Reykjavík honoured an unknown office worker instead. A man in a coat strides toward City Hall with a briefcase, and above the waist he is a block of raw rock. It stands by the pond and costs nothing to see.
- [Höfði House, Reykjavík: the 1986 Reagan Gorbachev summit](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/hofdi-house): Höfði is the white timber house on the Reykjavík shore where Reagan and Gorbachev met in 1986. The talks ended without an agreement and are now remembered as the moment the Cold War began to come apart. You can walk up to it freely; the inside is not open to visitors.
- [Harpa Concert Hall, Reykjavík: the hall that almost fell](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/harpa): Harpa is the coloured glass concert hall on the Reykjavík harbour. It stood half built when the banks fell in 2008, and the country finished it anyway. The ground floor is open to anyone, free, and the facade changes with the weather and the hour.
- [Alþingi Parliament House, Austurvöllur, Reykjavík](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/althingi): The plain grey house on Austurvöllur holds Alþingi, a parliament first gathered in the year 930, which makes it one of the oldest in the world. Four guardian spirits of Iceland are carved above its windows. You look at it from the square, free.
- [The Partnership Sculpture on the Reykjavík shore](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/partnership-sculpture): The Partnership is two bronze figures leaning into each other on the Sæbraut shore path. The American ambassador Charles Cobb and his wife Sue gave it to Reykjavík in 1991, fifty years after Iceland and the United States opened relations. Pétur Bjarnason made it, and an identical version stands in Miami.
- [Hallgrímskirkja, Reykjavík: the church shaped like lava](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/hallgrimskirkja): Hallgrímskirkja took more than forty years to build, and its front was shaped to echo the basalt columns of the Icelandic coast. The church is free to enter; the tower, with the view over the coloured roofs, is the part you pay for.
- [The Sun Voyager (Sólfar), Reykjavík: not a Viking ship](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/sun-voyager): The Sun Voyager on the Reykjavík waterfront is not a Viking ship. Jón Gunnar Árnason meant it as a dream boat, an ode to the sun, and it has faced Mount Esja across the bay since 1990. It is free to visit and open at every hour.
- [The Water Carrier Statue, Lækjargata, Reykjavík](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/water-carrier): The Water Carrier near Lækjargata is a bronze woman bent under a yoke with a pail at each end, the work women did before Reykjavík had pipes. Ásmundur Sveinsson shaped her in the nineteen thirties and the city argued for years about whether she was too plain to stand. She was placed in the late forties.
- [Grótta Lighthouse, Reykjavík: walking there at low tide](https://kyrrd.pics/journal/grotta-lighthouse): Grótta is a small island with a white lighthouse at the western tip of Seltjarnarnes, reachable on foot only for a few hours around low tide, across a sandbar that floods faster than most people expect. The present lighthouse went up in 1947. The island is a nature reserve and closes for nesting from about the start of May to the middle of July.

## Photographs
- [The Sun Voyager](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/sun-voyager): Not the Viking ship everyone takes it for, Jón Gunnar Árnason’s steel Sun Voyager has faced Mount Esja across the bay since 1990.
- [Government House](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/government-house): White above the Lækjargata lawn, Government House, the prime minister’s seat in a stone building raised in the 1760s as the country’s prison.
- [Himinglæva](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/wind-harp): A steel wave the wind plays on the square outside Harpa, Elín Hansdóttir’s Himinglæva, the concert hall’s own instrument.
- [Skúli Magnússon](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/skuli-magnusson): Father of Reykjavík in bronze, Skúli Magnússon, whose Aðalstræti workshops turned a scatter of farms into a town.
- [Grotta Lighthouse](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/grotta-lighthouse): Reachable on foot only around low tide, the Grótta lighthouse on an island the sea cuts off twice a day.
- [Christian IX](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/christian-ix): Arm held out on the Government House lawn, Christian IX of Denmark, offering Iceland the constitution he brought over in 1874.
- [The Cellist](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/cellist): Bowing a cello with no strings in the water outside Harpa, Ólöf Pálsdóttir’s Musician, modelled on the cellist Erling Blöndal Bengtsson.
- [Althingi Parliament House](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/althingi): Behind a plain grey façade on Austurvöllur sits Alþingi, a parliament first gathered in the year 930.
- [Íslandsvarðan](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/islandsvardan): Cast to look like raw lava, Íslandsvarðan, Jóhann Eyfells’s bronze cairn with a hole that keeps Mount Esja in view.
- [Water Carrier](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/water-carrier): Bowed under a wooden yoke, the Water Carrier who hauled Reykjavík’s water by hand long before the pipes arrived.
- [Leif Eiríksson](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/leif-eriksson): On a stone ship’s prow before Hallgrímskirkja, Leif Eiríksson, the son of Iceland who reached America five centuries before Columbus.
- [The Berlin Wall](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/berlin-wall): A painted slab of the Berlin Wall on the lawn by Höfði, set down where Reagan and Gorbachev began the thaw that brought it down.
- [Hallgrimskirkja](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/hallgrimskirkja): Forty years in the building, Hallgrímskirkja’s pale tower was shaped after the basalt columns of the Icelandic coast.
- [Jón Sigurðsson](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/jon-sigurdsson): Facing the parliament from his column on Austurvöllur, Jón Sigurðsson, the man who argued Iceland back to itself.
- [Höfði Lighthouse](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/hofdi-lighthouse): Bright yellow on its viewing platform by Höfði, a lighthouse built in 2019 to the pattern of the old harbour lights of 1917.
- [Unknown Bureaucrat](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/unknown-bureaucrat): Sharp from the waist down and a raw block of basalt above, the Unknown Bureaucrat, a monument to the official no one remembers.
- [Domkirkjan](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/domkirkjan): Beside the parliament on Austurvöllur, the cathedral where members still gather for a service before each new session opens.
- [Öndvegissúlur](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/ondvegissulur): Copper pillars crowned with carved forms beside Höfði, Sigurjón Ólafsson’s monument to the high seat pillars Ingólfur threw into the sea.
- [The Partnership Sculpture](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/partnership-sculpture): Two bronze figures leaning into each other on the shore, the Partnership, a gift between Iceland and the United States.
- [Hannes Hafstein](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/hannes-hafstein): Open handed on the Government House lawn, Hannes Hafstein, the poet who became the first Icelander to govern Iceland from the house behind him.
- [Víkurgarður](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/vikurgardur): Three stones carved with the faint figures of the parish, marking Víkurgarður, the churchyard where Reykjavík buried its dead for six centuries.
- [Harpa](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/harpa): Coloured glass that shifts with the weather, Harpa on the old harbour, left half built when the banks fell and finished anyway.
- [Einar Benediktsson](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/einar-benediktsson): Poet, lawyer and tireless schemer, Einar Benediktsson stands beside Höfði, the man who, the story goes, once tried to sell the northern lights.
- [Séra Bjarni Jónsson](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/sera-bjarni): Beside the cathedral he served for forty years, séra Bjarni Jónsson, the priest all of Reykjavík knew by sight.
- [Ingibjörg H. Bjarnason](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/ingibjorg-bjarnason): Beside the parliament she entered first, Ingibjörg H. Bjarnason, headmistress, suffragist and the first woman elected to the Alþingi.
- [The Black Cone](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/black-cone): Driven into a split boulder outside parliament, the Black Cone, Iceland’s stark monument to the right to protest.
- [Úr Álögum](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/ur-alogum): Sword lowered over a beaten shape, Einar Jónsson’s Úr álögum, the moment a spell breaks in the garden below Hallgrímskirkja.
- [Hofdi House](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/hofdi-house): On the north shore stands Höfði, the white house where Reagan and Gorbachev met in 1986 and the Cold War began to thaw.
- [Ingólfsgarður Lighthouse](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/ingolfsgardur-lighthouse): Bright yellow at the end of a stone breakwater, the little lighthouse marking the mouth of Reykjavík’s old harbour.
- [Jón Vídalín](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/jon-vidalin): In the ruff of his office beside Dómkirkjan, Jón Vídalín, the bishop whose book of sermons was read aloud in Icelandic homes for two centuries.
- [Ingólfur Arnarson](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/ingolfur-arnarson): Spear in hand on his green hill, Ingólfur Arnarson, the settler the sagas credit with founding Reykjavík.
- [Shore Piece](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/shore-piece): A run of boulders polished to a shine among the rough rock of the Sæbraut seawall, Sigurður Guðmundsson’s Fjöruverk, hiding in plain sight since 2002.
- [Looking Seawards](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/looking-seawards): Two fishermen in oilskins reading the horizon by the old harbour, Looking Seawards, Ingi P. Gíslason’s 1997 tribute to the men who worked the sea.
- [The Settlement Pillars](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/settlement-pillars): A basalt pillar downtown, a steel pipe breathing steam beside it, marking where Ingólfur’s high seat pillars are said to have washed ashore and Reykjavík began.
- [Ólafur Thors](https://kyrrd.pics/plate/olafur-thors): By Tjarnargata stands Ólafur Thors, cast by Sigurjón Ólafsson: the shipping tycoon’s son who became Iceland’s prime minister six times.

## Guides
- [The Long Walk](https://kyrrd.pics/walk): a free self-guided walk through Reykjavík, 30 stops in seven chapters, 5.5 km, with the distances and the practical details measured on foot.

## About
- [How it works](https://kyrrd.pics/about): choose a photograph, add your words, send it as a signed digital card.
